title: the Devi Mahatmya (13 chapters, read whole)
hook: the book ends where it began: the king and the merchant go to a riverbank, and the goddess asks what each one wants

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, Shumbha said the goddess fought with borrowed strength, and she answered: I am alone here in the world. When something hard ended, did you notice what went quiet? Today, the last pages. Day one thousand seventy-one.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `I AM ALONE HERE IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Remember the forest? A king who'd lost his kingdom. A merchant thrown out by his own family. Both unable to stop worrying, both asking a sage why knowing doesn't help. On the first day of this year, the Devi Mahatmya began with them. Every story since, the sleeping Vishnu, the buffalo, Kali, Raktabija, Shumbha, has been the sage's answer to the king's question: who is this goddess? Now the battles are done. One more hymn, one more promise, and then the book walks back into the forest, to the two men who were listening the whole time. What will they do with what they've heard?
screen: `BACK TO THE FOREST.` → `EVERY STORY WAS AN ANSWER.` → `WHAT WILL THEY DO WITH IT?`

segments.voice: First, the eleventh chapter. After Shumbha falls, the gods praise the goddess one more time, calling her Narayani, and asking her to be gracious to the whole world. And she gives them a promise bigger than before. In paraphrase: whenever trouble rises from the demons, I will come down and destroy the enemy. She even names future appearances. In one, during a terrible drought, she says she will feed the world with plants grown from her own body, and be called Shakambhari, she who bears the greens. Then the twelfth chapter, where she tells the gods what hearing this story brings to those who recite it and listen. And then the thirteenth, the last. The sage Medhas finishes, and says to the king: this is the goddess I told you about. She is the one who draws you into confusion, and the one who can set you free. Go to her. So the king and the merchant go to a riverbank. They make an image of the goddess out of earth, and they worship her there, for a long time, with offerings and with their whole attention. And the goddess appears to them, and asks each what he wants. The king asks for his kingdom back, in this life, and a kingdom that won't be lost in the next. She grants it. The merchant, the one who couldn't stop worrying about the family that threw him out, asks for something else. In paraphrase: the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine. She grants that too. Two men, the same forest, the same stories, two different requests. The text doesn't rank them. The book that began with two worries ends with two answers.
screen: `THE GODDESS AS NARAYANI.` · `WHENEVER TROUBLE RISES, I WILL COME.` · `AN EARTH IMAGE BY A RIVER.` · `A KINGDOM, AND FREEDOM FROM I AND MINE.` · then, large: `TWO WORRIES, TWO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the goddess's question. Settle, and let the breath slow. Then let the question the goddess asks both men sit quietly in you: what do you want? Don't answer quickly. Let the first answer come, the practical one, the kingdom. Notice it, kindly. Then wait a little longer, and see if a quieter answer comes underneath, the merchant's kind. You don't have to choose between them. Just hear both. If you pray, you can bring both before the goddess, or God, in the words you already use. If you don't, let the question rest on the breath. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. The glory of the goddess, read whole: a book that begins with two men in a forest who can't let go, and ends with each of them asking her for what he wants.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, ask yourself once what you want, and wait for the second, quieter answer. Day one thousand seventy-one. The Devi Mahatmya, read whole.

howItsDone: Some Hindus who recite the whole Devi Mahatmya finish with the thirteenth chapter's boons to the king and the merchant, and the eleventh chapter's hymn to Narayani is also chanted on its own.

fork.setup: you're the merchant. your family threw you out, and you couldn't stop worrying about them. now the goddess stands in front of you and asks what you want. what do you ask?
options: my wealth and my family back.
the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine.
fork.reveal: the merchant asks for the knowledge that frees him from I and mine. the king asks for his kingdom. the goddess grants both.

original.note: Sanskrit: Nārāyaṇī, a name of the goddess in the gods' hymn of the eleventh chapter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle book that ends when the last demon dies.
what it means: the stories were a sage's answer to a king's question; the book ends back in the forest, with two men asking the goddess for two different things.
what a scholar hears: the frame closes in chapter 13: Suratha and Samādhi worship an earthen image, and receive a kingdom and liberating knowledge.

notes: Last of the ten Devi Mahatmya days; covers chapters 11–13 and closes the frame opened on 1062.

Ch. 11 paraphrased: the gods praise her as Nārāyaṇī (the sarvamaṅgala-māṅgalye verse is in this hymn, not quoted); her promise (itthaṃ yadā yadā bādhā dānavotthā bhaviṣyati / tadā tadāvatīryāhaṃ kariṣyāmy arisaṃkṣayam); Śākambharī during a drought, nourishing the world with life-sustaining vegetables grown from her own body. The text's other named future forms (born of Yashoda, Raktadantika, Shatakshi, Durga, Bhima, Bhramari) are not named. Confirm.

Ch. 12 summarized in one sentence. Ch. 13: Medhas's closing words, the riverbank, the earthen image, worship (the text gives a length of time, not spoken), the boons: the king his kingdom in this life and an imperishable one hereafter (and rebirth as Manu Sāvarṇi, not mentioned); the merchant the knowledge that destroys the attachment of 'I' and 'mine' (mamāham iti). Confirm.
Practice draws on the goddess asking each man what he wants; it does not rank the two requests, as the text doesn't. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with 'the text doesn't rank them'.
